title: Sustained growth of quantum circuit complexity in many-body Hamiltonian dynamics
authors: Wonjun Lee, Saúl Pilatowsky-Cameo, Soonwon Choi
abstract: The quantum circuit complexity of an evolving many-body quantum system is believed to exhibit a sustained growth, maintained for timescales much longer than the onset of thermalization. Most previous works have focused on models which violate energy conservation, such as random unitary circuits. Here we study generic, local time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics. We unconditionally prove that for generic local Hamiltonians and typical initial product states at high effective temperature, the robust quantum circuit complexity must grow over a very long period of time, attaining an exponentially large value at late times. Our approach relies on two structural properties that we prove rigorously: (i) generic local Hamiltonians satisfy generalized spectral no-resonance conditions of arbitrary order, and (ii) typical high-temperature product states are effectively supported in exponentially many energy eigenstates. These properties have been widely assumed without proof in prior works. As corollaries of this result, we show the late-time state displays robust volume-law entanglement that is irremovable by polynomial-size circuits, and we establish a no fast-forwarding result for generic local Hamiltonians. We also lower bound the complexity of preparing sufficiently large subsystems with local quantum channels, in contrast with sufficiently small thermalizing regions which we show retain low complexity at late times.
summary: This paper proves that for generic, energy-conserving quantum systems, the quantum circuit complexity of large subsystems grows exponentially over extremely long timescales, persisting long after the system has reached apparent thermal equilibrium. The result hinges on proving deep structural properties of local Hamiltonians and initial states. It establishes that the dynamics are computationally complex even when the system appears simple locally.
main_problem: To determine if the quantum circuit complexity of an evolving many-body quantum system exhibits sustained growth for timescales much longer than the onset of thermalization, particularly for energy-conserving dynamics.
main_result: The quantum circuit complexity of subsystems in generic local Hamiltonian dynamics is proven to grow exponentially over very long timescales, even after the system appears to have thermalized.
method: The proof relies on rigorously establishing two structural properties of generic local Hamiltonians and high-temperature product states: generalized spectral no-resonance conditions and effective support in exponentially many energy eigenstates.
model_or_system: The study concerns many-body quantum systems evolving unitarily under generic, local, time-independent, and extensive Hamiltonians on a Euclidean lattice of qubits.
key_observables: Quantum Circuit Complexity ($C_\epsilon$), robust volume-law entanglement, and the time scale of complexity growth.
important_parameters: High effective temperature ($ eta=0$ or $| eta| <  eta_c$), subsystem size $|A|$, and the time elapsed $t$.
main_assumptions: The Hamiltonian must be generic (satisfying spectral no-resonance conditions) and the initial state must be typical (energy dispersed).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that circuit complexity continues to grow post-thermalization. Figure 2 summarizes the logical flow connecting assumptions, derived properties, main results, and implications.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the necessity of structural properties (spectral conditions, state support) and then using these to prove the exponential growth of complexity (Theorem 1). It contrasts this with saturation for small subsystems and establishes related results like no fast-forwarding.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, non-trivial lower bound on the computational complexity of quantum states generated by local Hamiltonians, extending the understanding of quantum information retention far beyond simple thermalization timescales.

At thermal- ization, entanglement saturates and the state becomes locally indistinguishable from the Gibbs state, but nevertheless the state continues to evolve. We show that quantum circuit com- plexity continues to grow for a very long period of time, even after the onset of thermalization.

FIG. 2. Logical structure of the main results. Orange boxes denote assumptions, green boxes denote derived prop- erties, blue boxes denote main results in this work, and dark- blue boxes denote implications of our results.

FIG. 3. Main counting argument. Set SG of states that can be prepared by a sequence of G two-qubit channels (green) and its covering net with states σi (orange circles). The system is initialized in a product state (black circle) which evolves in time (arrow). At time t, the circuit com- plexity is ≤G only if |ψ(t)⟩is within the neighborhood of some σi. We bound the fraction of time that |ψ(t)⟩can spend near a particular σi (red) to be double-exponentially small, so a union bound guarantees that the total time spent inside the green region is double-exponentially small, as long as G is exponential.
